screens.h: Electrons are a reactant you can count
p: Every electron that reaches the cathode reduces part of a Cu²⁺ ion, so the **mass** of copper depends on the **charge** that flowed. One mole of electrons carries 96 500 C: the **Faraday constant**.
**q = It** (time in seconds) and **q = nF**, where n is the number of moles of **electrons** and F = 96 500 C·mol⁻¹ (on the data sheet).
Read Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu as a balanced equation: 1 mol Cu²⁺ reacts with 2 mol e⁻ and gives 1 mol Cu.
Run it left to right (mass → time) or right to left (current and time → mass). The **ratio from the half-reaction** is the link the 2025 report says candidates still leave out.

rules: Write the **half-reaction** at the electrode. It gives the ratio: Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag (1 e⁻ per Ag); Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (2 e⁻ per Cu); 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ (4 e⁻ per O₂).
Convert what you know to moles: n = m/M, n = V/V_{m} or n(e⁻) = q/F.
Use the ratio to go between moles of **electrons** and moles of **substance**.
Finish with q = It (time in **seconds**), m = nM or V = nV_{m}.

screens.q: 0,2 mol of electrons reach the cathode of a copper cell: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. How many moles of copper are deposited?

traps: Cu²⁺ + **2**e⁻ → Cu: each Cu needs two electrons, so 0,2 mol of electrons deposits only 0,1 mol of copper.
Each Cu needs two electrons, so there are fewer moles of copper than of electrons: divide by 2.
num.hint: Each Cu needs two electrons: n(Cu) = ½n(e⁻).

screens.why: Cu²⁺ + **2**e⁻ → Cu: each Cu needs two electrons, so 0,2 mol of electrons deposits only **0,1** mol of copper. “Many candidates are still neglecting to use the ratio in the half-reaction.” (IEB Examiners’ Report 2025)

traps: That is n(Cu). First find the moles of **electrons**: n(e⁻) = q/F.

screens.q: In the baby-shoe cell (29.4), 15,9 g of copper is deposited on the shoe (IEB May 2026 P2 Q7.3.5). (a) Calculate the number of moles of electrons that must be supplied. (b) A constant current of 20 A was used. Calculate the time taken.

traps: That is n(Cu). Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu: each Cu needs two electrons, so n(e⁻) = 2n(Cu).
Each Cu needs two electrons, so there are MORE moles of electrons than of copper: n(e⁻) = 2n(Cu).

ask.prompt: Work out the time, in seconds.

traps: That is in minutes. Give the time in seconds: t = q/I.
Check n(e⁻): Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so n(e⁻) = 2n(Cu) = 0,500788 mol.

screens.h: Worked example 29.13: gas volumes from the electrolysis of water
screens.q: Dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed with platinum electrodes. A current of 2,00 A flows for 32 minutes 10 seconds. Calculate the volume of (a) oxygen and (b) hydrogen produced, both measured at STP.

traps: That is in minutes. Time must be in seconds: 32 × 60 + 10.
O₂ needs **4**e⁻: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻, so n(O₂) = ¼n(e⁻).
Use the ratio: O₂ needs 4e⁻, so n(O₂) = ¼n(e⁻) = 0,0100 mol.

screens.note: The same charge gives twice the volume of hydrogen as of oxygen, because O₂ needs 4e⁻ and H₂ needs 2e⁻.

screens.h: Cells in series: the same charge
p: When two electrolytic cells are connected in **series**, the same current flows through both for the same time, so the **same charge** and the same number of moles of electrons pass through each.

Electrons move only in the wires and electrodes, and ions carry the charge in each solution. The same charge passes through both cells, so the same number of moles of electrons is transferred at the electrodes of each cell.

screens.q: A CuSO₄ cell and a AgNO₃ cell are in series. 1,08 g of silver is deposited. Calculate the mass of copper deposited.

traps: Cu²⁺ + **2**e⁻ → Cu: n(Cu) = ½n(e⁻). (Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag gives n(e⁻) = n(Ag) = 0,0100 mol.)
Cu²⁺ + **2**e⁻ → Cu: n(Cu) = ½n(e⁻). (Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag gives n(e⁻) = n(Ag) = 0,0100 mol.)
The same charge passes through both cells, so the same **moles of electrons** are transferred in each, not the same mass.
